title: How to Watch Billy Evans’ First TV Interview About ‘You Can See Everything’ Online
description:

	Billy Eva
body:
If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission.

	Billy Evans is speaking out about his portrayal in Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s hit documentary “You Can See Everything.”

	The longtime partner of disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes sits down with CBS News chief correspondent Matt Gutman for his first television interview on “CBS News Sunday Morning,” airing Sunday, Nov. 15, at 9 a.m. ET/PT on CBS and streaming on Paramount+.


	The interview arrives amid renewed public fascination with Holmes and Evans following the A24’s breakout documentary, which follows the couple in the weeks leading up to Holmes’ imprisonment for defrauding Theranos investors. The film has become a box office sensation, grossing more than $80 million worldwide.
	

	“I would have preferred for that not to be the case, but it’s entertainment. I didn’t get to control that edit,” Evans tells Gutman in a preview of Sunday’s interview. He adds that his primary motivation for participating was to show audiences a more personal side of Holmes, who is currently serving a federal prison sentence for fraud.

	Viewers can watch the interview live on Paramount+ with a Premium subscription, which costs $13.99 per month and includes access to a live feed of their local CBS station. The streaming service’s ad-supported Essential plan, priced at $8.99 per month, also offers CBS programming on demand, with new episodes generally available the day after broadcast.

	Sunday’s broadcast, hosted by Jane Pauley, will also feature interviews with U2 marking the band’s 50th anniversary, John Travolta discussing his upcoming film “November 1963” and author Min Jin Lee on her latest novel, “American Hagwon.”

title: Jakarta World Cinema Expands to Malang and Bandung, Where Palme d’Or Winner ‘Fjord’ Opens Festival
description: Jakarta World Cinema has taken its festival outside the Indonesian capital for the first time, with the inaugural Bandung World Cinema and Malang W
body:
Jakarta World Cinema has taken its festival outside the Indonesian capital for the first time, with the inaugural Bandung World Cinema and Malang World Cinema opening simultaneously on Nov. 14 in two cities with large student populations and busy creative scenes.

	Bandung’s screenings are taking place at CGV Paris Van Java, while Malang’s are at Cinépolis Malang Town Square, with both editions running through Nov. 21. The move takes the festival to audiences who have tracked the Jakarta event from elsewhere in the country.
	

	The Bandung edition is programming 203 international titles drawn from 69 countries. Cristian Mungiu’s “Fjord,” which won this year’s Palme d’Or at Cannes, opened proceedings.

	Also on the slate are Beth de Araujo’s “Josephine,” which took both the Grand Jury Prize and the Audience Award in Sundance’s U.S. Dramatic Competition in 2026, and Marine Atlan’s “La Gradiva,” winner of the AMI Paris Grand Prize at this year’s Cannes Critics’ Week. Sandra Wollner’s “Everytime,” which picked up the Un Certain Regard Prize at Cannes, screens alongside Kurosawa Kiyoshi’s new feature “The Samurai and the Prisoner,” a Cannes Premiere selection.

	The festival’s online program, available until Nov. 21, includes Ildiko Enyedi’s “Silent Friend,” a Fipresci Prize winner at Venice in 2025, and Ilker Çatak’s “Yellow Letters,” this year’s Golden Bear winner at the Berlinale.

	Bandung Mayor Muhammad Farhan attended the opening night at CGV Paris Van Java.

	“Bandung World Cinema gives the local audience an unprecedented opportunity to watch alternative cinema outside of the mainstream Hollywood films that dominate the theaters. The hope is that this festival will foster a greater local appreciation for film, become a source of inspiration for cinephiles, and encourage aspiring filmmakers to pursue their dreams,” Farhan said.
	

	Frederica, executive director of Bandung World Cinema, said organizers had noticed keen interest from cinephiles beyond Jakarta for years. “Bringing the Jakarta World Cinema experience to Bandung and Malang for the first time has been a long time coming,” she said. “Over the next eight days, audiences in both cities will experience the exact same caliber of bold, thought-provoking, and celebrated global cinema that defines JWC.”

	Unlike the Jakarta event, Bandung will wrap on Nov. 21 with a free open-air screening for the general public. The outdoor program will feature work by students at Bandung universities and winners of the KlikFilm Short Movie Competition, before closing with a restored version of “Lewat Djam Malam” (“After the Curfew”), Usmar Ismail’s 1954 Indonesian classic.

title: Seville European Film Festival Prizes: ‘You Don’t Belong Here,’ ‘Falling House,’ ’Adult Supervision’ Win Big
description: Romania’s Florin Şerban added a Seville Golden Giraldillo to a Golden Leopard at Locarno on Saturday, winning Best Film in main competition at the
body:
Romania’s Florin Şerban added a Seville Golden Giraldillo to a Golden Leopard at Locarno on Saturday, winning Best Film in main competition at the 2026 Seville European Film Festival which also prized Venice New Horizons buzz title “Falling House” and Sweden’s Oscar entry “Adult Supervision.”

	Seville’s biggest world premiere, Spain’s “The Director,” also scored a high profile award at a festival which works at multiple levels: a new talent springboard, an industry hub, further recognition for the large number ofEuropean films which partly fly under the radar, and a springboard for European productions breaking out to international sales or consolidating their contention for Oscar International Feature Film shortlist recognition.
	

	Notably, victors at Seville’s Saturday’s prize announcement also took in Marcus Schleinzer’s Austrian Oscar entry “Rose” and Abinash Bikram Shah’s “Elephants in the Fog,” a submission from Nepal.

	A closer look at Seville main competition winners:

	“You Don’t Belong Here,” (Florin Şerban)

	Described by Variety as “a somber study of anti-Roma racism in the country, “You Don’t Belong Here” marks the fourth feature from Şerban whose 2010 debut, “If I Want to Whistle, I Whistle,” took a Berlinale Grand Prix.

	Shot in hallmark drab Romanian cinema tones, which won Bogdan Ionescu Best Artistic Direction, “You Don’t Belong Here” turns on a respected, upright surgeon who discovers his son has helped beat to death a Roma man. Filmed in static shoots with pauses between dialog, the film won four awards at Locarno, including but, as Variety noted at Locarno, failed to impress Variety critic Jay Weissberg who lamented that the film “opens with great promise and finishes with a stupefyingly misguided coda.”
	

	“Falling House,” (Mohsen Gharaei)

	Another tale of threatened patriarchy, Iranian filmmaker Mohsen Gharaei’s “Falling House” scored Seville’s Grand Jury Prize, plus a nod for Best Editing for Evelyn Rack and Emad Khodabakhsh. Bowing in Venice Horizons, and described by the director as a story about “lost freedom,” it turns on a prison guard who, learning his eldest daughter plans to escape to Turkey for a career in modelling, incarcerates his own family in a house facing demolition.

	Sold by Paradise City Sales. “Falling House” has closed a first batch of deals with France’s Jokers Films for France, Italy’s Wanted Cinema and Karma Films for Spain.

	“Adult Supervision,” (Alex Schulman)

	Much of Seville’s focus is on new or emerging talent. Of all its feature debuts, the biggest winner was “Adult Supervision,” from well-known Swedish author and podcast host Alex Schulman which has has sold widely by Heretic, including to WBD, Place and Vertigo. The film’s double wins – a Puerta América Award and Best Actor prize – will stoke more word around Sweden’s International Feature Oscar entry, which was another buzz title which has struck promising first sales, selling widely for Heretic, including to WBD, Place and Vertigo.

	“El Director,” (Dani de la Orden, Spain)

	Seville’s biggest new push at Frame, its industry umbrella, saw it partner with Spain’s ICAA film agency to launch Insula, a screenplay market featuring 58 titles. Its jury president this year was AMPAS VP Howard A. Rodman, a screenwriter best known for “Savage Grace” and “August,” So Best Screenplay was a key plaudit, which went to a film where words are crucial: Dani de la Orden’s “El Director,” based on David Jiménez’s lid-lifting autobiographical non-fiction book about his time as editor-in-chief at newspaper El Mundo, and his battle to protect riotous journalism against the vested economic and political interests to often served. The prize went more specifically to two institutions on Spain’s film-TV scene: Alejandro Hernández, a co-writer on films and series by Alejandro Amenábar (“The Captive”) and Mariano Barroso (“The Farad”) and Michel Gaztambide, who broke out co-writing Julio Medem’s debut “Cows,” back in 1992, before penning many of the films and series by Enrique Urbizu plus Victor Erice’s 2023 “Close Your Eyes.”
	

	“Children of the Monkey,” (Tomasso Landucci)

	The Seville European Film Festival also highlights movies which merit more recognition. One case in point: Tomasso Landucci’s Venice Horizons Best Screenplay and Best Actor (Riccardo Scamarcio) winner “Children of the Monkey,” which this time round at Seville scored Best Director. In its portrayal of the dilemma of the father of a disabled son, “Children of the Monkey” is both deeply felt and impressively sensitive in the way it explores his painful emotional predicament,”Diego Lerer, one of the critics who did catch the film in Venice, wrote in his blog Micropsia.

	“Wild Is the Wind,” (“Tralovento,” Eloy Domínguez Serén)

	A second prize for Spain: Galician actress Melania Cruz (“Gangs of Galicia”) won her biggest prize to date, scooping best actress for her lead turn in “Wild With the Wind.” the feature debut of Eloy Domínguez Serén, from a screenplay co-written with top Catalan auteur Meritxell Colell (“Far From the Trees”). Cruz plays Ana, who returns to her home village in rural Galicia after her father’s death, but stays to oppose a utility company’s plans to build a wind farm on community land. Bowing at Mexico’s Morelia Festival, the film won praise, such as in aCriticalia.com review, for its measured pace. Cruz’s performance and nuanced view of the wind farm project.

	A list of winners at the 23rd Seville European Film Festival, 2026:

	OFFICIAL SELECTION

	Golden Giraldillo for Best Film:“You Don’t Belong Here,” (written and directed by Florin Şerban, Romania)

	Grand Jury Award: “Falling House,” (Mohsen Gharaei, written with Amir Mohammad Abdi, Irán)

	Puerta América Award: “Adult Supervision,” (written and directed by Alex Schulman)

	Special Mention, Puerta América Award: “Rose,” by Markus Schleinzer, co-written with Alexander Brom

	Best Direction: “Children of the Monkey,” (Tommaso Landucci, co-written with Damiano Femfert, Italy)

	Best Screenplay: Michel Gaztambide, Alejandro Hernández for “El Director,” directed by Dani de la Orden, Spain)

	Best Actress: Melania Cruz for “Tralovento,”

	Best Actor: Gustaf Skarsgård, Fares Fares y Linus Wahlgren for

	“Adult Supervision”
	

	Best Editing: Evelyn Rack y Emad Khodabakhsh for “Falling House”

	Best Cinematography: Noé Bach for “Elephants in the Fog.”

	Best Art Direction: Bogdan Ionescu for “You Don’t Belong Here”

	OFFICIAL SELECTION SHORT FILMS

	Live Action: “Fresh Cut,” directed by Hadrien Bels, co-written with Jasmine Badr

	Animation: “Gently,” written and directed by Jamaica Kindlová

	EMBRUJO

	Best Film Award: “Revolutionaries Never Die,” Mohanad Yaqubi cwritten with Mathilde Rouxel

	RAMPA

	Best Film Award; “House of the Wind,” directed and written by

	Auguste Bernard Kouemo Yanghu

	ALUMBRAMIENTO

	Best Film Award: “Four Minus Three,” Adrian Goiginger, co-written with Senad Halilbašić.

	PANORAMA ANDALUZ

	Juan Antonio Bermúdez Best Film Award: “A Man on a Bridge,” written and directed by David Martín de los Santos.

	Best Documentary Award: “Como todo mortal,” written and directed by María Molina Peiró.

	Jury Special Mention: “200 Lives: Paco Rabal,” written and directed by Vanessa Benítez

	Audience Award for Best Film, EFA Selection: “Coward,” Lukas Dhont written with Angelo Tijssens.

	Film Lovers of the Future Award: “In Waves,” by Phuong Mai Nguyen from a screenplay by Fanny Burdino and Samuel Doux, based on a graphic novel by AJ Dungo.

title: Thessaloniki Awards: Jacqueline Lentzou’s ‘A Day in the Life of Jo: Chapter Phaedra’ Wins the Golden Alexander
description: Jacqueline Lentzou’s “A Day in the Life of Jo: Chapter Phaedra” won the top prize Sunday at the Thessaloniki Film Festival, taking home the Golden
body:
Jacqueline Lentzou’s “A Day in the Life of Jo: Chapter Phaedra” won the top prize Sunday at the Thessaloniki Film Festival, taking home the Golden Alexander for best feature film in the Arrivals international competition section.

	The Greek filmmaker’s sophomore feature premiered in the Venice Film Festival’s Horizons strand, where it won the award for best director. It’s since gone on to play at the New York Film Festival, the BFI London Film Festival and the Busan Film Festival.
	

	Inspired by true events, “A Day in the Life of Jo” follows the unruly, melancholic 15-year-old Jo — played by newcomer Evia Andriopoulou — as she navigates the ups and downs of a typical day in a typical teenager’s life. Drifting through a series of seemingly unrelated and inconsequential events, that otherwise ordinary day is turned upside-down with the arrival of Phaedra (Anastasia Gouliamou), a bookish classmate whose warbling rendition of an old love ballad reduces Jo to tears. In an instant, her life — her drab, unremarkable day — becomes full of possibility, hurtling toward both tragedy and transformation.

	The film scooped a trio of awards on Sunday, as well as a Special Mention for Andriopoulou.

	The Silver Alexander for best director went to Pauline Julier and Nicolas Chapoulier for “Les Indes,” which had its premiere in the Venice Film Festival’s Venice Days strand. The writer-director duo’s feature debut is set in 1652 and follows three men as they transport a painting across a Europe ravaged by wars and uprisings.

	Best acting honors in the Arrivals competition went to Caique Copque and Italo Martins for “The Riverbank,” a queer erotic thriller from Brazilian directors Matheus Farias and Enock Carvalho that premiered in competition in Locarno. Best actress went to Arisa Sasaki, for Konstantina Kotzamani’s Cannes Un Certain Regard-premiering debut feature “Titanic Ocean,” an offbeat coming-of-age story set at a boarding school for aspiring mermaids in Japan.
	

	In the festival’s Meet the Neighbors+ competition section, which includes debut or sophomore films from the 36 countries of Southeastern Europe, the Mediterranean and the Middle East, the Golden Alexander for best feature went to “Dua,” by Kosovan filmmaker Blerta Basholli. Premiering in Cannes’ Critics’ Week strand, the director’s sophomore feature tells the story of a 13-year-old girl coming of age in the shadow of the Kosovo War.

	The section’s Silver Alexander for best director went to Abdallah Alkhatib for “Chronicles From the Siege.” The winner of the Berlinale’s Perspectives award for debuts, the film presents vignettes of Palestinian lives in Gaza and in refugee camps.

	The award for best actor went to Alexis Manenti and Julian Świeżewski for “Flesh and Fuel,” French filmmaker Pierre Le Gall’s story about a passionate love affair between two long-distance truck drivers. Premiering in Cannes’ Critics Week, it took the top prize at the Zurich Film Festival and also earned Le Gall an award for best screenplay Sunday in Thessaloniki. Maria Petrova, the young star of Cypriot filmmaker Myrsini Aristidou’s Sundance Audience Prize-winning “Hold Onto Me,” took home the award for best actress.

	In the Film Forward competition section showcasing innovative filmmaking, the Golden Alexander went to Hoda Taheri and Boris Hadžija’s “I Plant My Hand in the Garden,” while the Silver Alexander went to Rob Rice for “Ponderosa,” whose star Alexis Blendel won the prize for best actress. The award for Best Artistic Achievement went to Argyris Germanidis’ “Particles of Dust,” while best actor honors went to Alexis Kalofolias for “Under the Judas Tree.”

	Here’s a rundown of the winners in the Thessaloniki Film Festival’s three competition sections:

	Arrivals

	Golden Alexander: “A Day in the Life of Jo: Chapter Phaedra,” Jacqueline Lentzou

	Silver Alexander: Pauline Julier and Nicolas Chapoulier, “Les Indes”

	Best actor: Caique Copque and Italo Martins, “The Riverbank”

	Best actress: Arisa Sasaki, “Titanic Ocean”

	Special Mention: Evita Andriopoulou, “A Day in the Life of Jo: Chapter Phaedra”

	Meet the Neighbors+

	Golden Alexander: “Dua,” Blerta Basholli
	

	Silver Alexander: Abdallah Alkhatib, “Chronicles From the Siege”

	Best actor: Alexis Manenti and Julian Świeżewski, “Flesh and Fuel”

	Best actress: Maria Petrova, “Hold Onto Me”

	Best screenplay: “Flesh and Fuel,” Pierre Le Gall

	Film Forward

	Golden Alexander: “I Plant My Hand in the Garden,” Hoda Taheri and Boris Hadžija

	Silver Alexander: Rob Rice, “Ponderosa”

	Best artistic achievement: “Particles of Dust,” Argyris Germanidis

	Best actress: Alexis Blendel, “Ponderosa”

	Best actor: Alexis Kalofolias, “Under the Judas Tree”

title: ‘Dhurandhar,’ ‘Kantara: A Legend – Chapter 1’ Among Indian Panorama Lineup at IFFI Goa
description: Aditya Dhar’s Hindi-language “Dhurandhar” will open the Indian Panorama section of the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Goa. Ris
body:
Aditya Dhar’s Hindi-language “Dhurandhar” will open the Indian Panorama section of the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Goa. Rishab Shetty’s Kannada-language “Kantara: A Legend – Chapter 1” is also in the lineup.

	Leena Yadav’s “Becoming,” in Ladakhi, will kick off the non-feature program. In all, IFFI’s annual survey of Indian filmmaking will present 25 features and 20 non-features this year.


	“Dhurandhar” and “Kantara: A Legend – Chapter 1” both sit in the five-title Mainstream Cinema strand. They are joined there by Samir Tewari’s Marathi-language film “Baapya,” Anil Ravipudi’s Telugu-language title “Mana Shankara Vara Prasad Garu (Pandaga Ki Vastunnaru)” and Pravin Vitthal Tarde’s “Deool Band 2,” also in Marathi.
	

	A 12-member jury chaired by Indian National Film Award-winning filmmaker Madhur Bhandarkar picked the features from 404 submissions. The other 20 titles cover 12 languages, from Hindi, Tamil and Bengali to Tulu and Nyishi.

	Among them are Kamakhya Narayan Singh’s “The Kerala Story 2 Goes Beyond,” Bharatbala Ganapathy’s “Banaras,” Akhil Sathyan’s Malayalam film “Sarvam Maya,” P. Sheshadri’s Kannada title “Ruby-Cube” and Singeetham Srinivasa Rao’s Telugu feature “Sing Geetham.” Sahil Shah’s “Birds on Ice,” in Ladakhi, and Duyu Tabyo’s Nyishi-language “Urum” also made the cut.

	The same jury shortlisted five films for IFFI’s best debut director of an Indian feature film award. The nominees are Ravi Varma Namburi’s “Chennai Love Story” (Telugu), Samarpan Sengupta’s “Pratyabartan” (Bengali), Jeejivisha Kale’s “Tighi” (Marathi), Raja Shabir Mohd Khan’s “Sledge” (Kashmiri) and Vishal Chaturvedi’s “Hanuman Ansh” (Hindi). The festival has also named five nominees for its best web series prize.
	

	On the non-feature side, a six-member jury led by director and educator Himanshu Sekhar Khatua whittled 358 entries down to 20. Picks include Bhasker Vishwanathan’s “The Unseen Holy River – Saraswati,” Aimee Baruah’s Assamese film “Red Carpet,” Suraj Kumar’s English-language “Nirmanjali: The Chandigarh of Maciej Nowicki” and Baba Tassaduq Hussain’s Kashmiri title “Naqsh-e-Daur.”

title: ‘Woman Unknown’ Breakout Mathilde Arcel on Her Venice Award-Winning Performance and Life After Her Lido Triumph: ‘Everything Is Open’
description:
Danish actress Mathilde Arcel would be the first to admit she didn’t see this coming.

	It’s been hardly two months since Arcel, in her first-ever
body:
Danish actress Mathilde Arcel would be the first to admit she didn’t see this coming.

	It’s been hardly two months since Arcel, in her first-ever leading role in a feature film, was awarded the Volpi Cup for best actress for her breakout performance in “Woman Unknown,” May el-Toukhy’s riveting, post-World War II drama that was also feted with the festival’s Golden Lion. Praised by Variety‘s Beatrice Loayza for her “magnetic” performance, Arcel plays a young housemaid whose intimate relationship with a German soldier during World War II threatens her future.
	

	Now, on the eve of the closing ceremony of the Thessaloniki Film Festival, which wraps Nov. 15 with el-Toukhy’s Venice winner, Arcel is taking in the news that she’s among the six nominees for best actress at the European Film Awards, whose nominations were announced Saturday afternoon in Thessaloniki.

	For Arcel, whose grandmother comes from the Greek island of Lesvos, the award ceremony, which will be held in Athens in January, feels like “a weird kind of homecoming.”

	“I feel so lucky,” she says.

	Over coffee at Thessaloniki’s Mediterranean Palace, the 30-year-old still seems awestruck by her meteoric rise. Just over two months ago, Arcel was herself a relative unknown, with a career that had mostly spanned the stage and television. Before her Venice breakout, her only appearances on the big screen were in supporting roles.

	After accepting best actress honors on the Lido, Arcel revealed to Danish media that she’d been collecting unemployment benefits ahead of the Italian fest; she was on her way to report to a job center in Copenhagen when she got word that she needed to fly back to Venice for the award ceremony.
	

	Reflecting in Thessaloniki on what she describes with wide eyes as “an adventure,” Arcel says, laughing, “It’s only downhill from here, right?”

	“Woman Unknown” draws on accounts of the many women across Europe who in peacetime were publicly shamed for their actions during the Nazi occupation — women whose stories have been swept to the margins of the collective memory of World War II. Accepting the Golden Lion in Venice, el-Touky acknowledged that the film had been “incredibly challenging to make financially, logistically, emotionally,” adding that “what kept me going was the urgent need to illuminate the unknown women of our common history, to make them known.”

	For Arcel, that history hit close to home.

	“I remember my Danish grandma, when I asked about the war, she told me that she was a kid on the day of the liberation, and she remembered that all of these women, her neighbors, were suddenly being pulled out onto the street. Other neighbors spitting at them, calling them names. Their hair was cut off,” Arcel says. “It really stuck with me, that this was…her most vivid memory from the occupation.”

	Still, until she began researching the part, the actress says she “didn’t know how vast this phenomenon was, all across Europe, how these women were treated.”



	

					Mathilde Arcel won the Volpi Cup for best actress at the Venice Film Festival.
									‘Woman Unknown’ Courtesy of Seminci
	



	In some ways, Arcel might have been destined for the part; after graduating from drama school in Copenhagen, she says, el-Toukhy was “the first person I wrote to.”

	“I wrote to her that I really loved her movies and I would love to work with her. I didn’t think it would happen,” she says. “But then she called me in for a casting. I definitely didn’t think I would get it, because I felt like the role had a different vibe to it than what I thought at that time was a natural fit for me…. It was very different from the parts I’d played. It was a new kind of challenge.”

	Her feelings changed once she unexpectedly landed the role, and she began to discuss the part with el-Toukhy. “When I read it, I couldn’t get a read on [the character of Marie] immediately,” she says. “It was kind of like detective work when I started working with her to see what kind of person she is and why she does what she does. It was intriguing.”
	

	As with the director’s 2019 drama “Queen of Hearts,” which stars Trine Dyrholm as a successful lawyer whose life gets turned upside down by an illicit affair, Arcel praises el-Toukhy for her ability to craft female characters “that are complex in their morality,” something that she describes as “quite rare.”

	Working with the Danish Egyptian filmmaker was a “very collaborative process,” she adds, describing the duo as “a good team.”

	“I wanted to know as much as I could about the period. What kind of dreams did they have at that time? What kind of movies did they watch? What kind of music did they hear?” Arcel says. “May is also very hands-on in the research. We both want to do everything we can to know as much as possible.”

	Next up for Arcel is a trip to the Marrakech Film Festival, where “Woman Unknown” plays in the festival’s Horizons section, while an Oscar campaign in the best international feature category is also underway, after Denmark selected the film as its submission for the 99th Academy Awards.

	Scripts have begun pouring in and the actress — who now has U.S. representation — has cleared her calendar for the next six months as she considers various offers.

	For now, it’s too soon to say what comes next. “It’s very different, very exciting,” she says. “It feels like being on the verge of something that might happen and might not even happen. A lot of dreams and hopes. Everything is open.”

	The Thessaloniki Film Festival runs Nov. 5 – 15.

schema.headline: ‘Woman Unknown’ Breakout Mathilde Arcel on Her Venice Award-Winning Performance and Life After Her Lido Triumph: ‘Everything Is Open’

title: John Mulaney Mocks Robert F. Kennedy Jr. in ‘SNL’ Monologue: ‘No One Likes Him. You Dumbass … Your Thing Can’t Be the Measles!’
description: John Mulaney‘s opening monologue on this week’s “Saturday Night Live” took an unexpected turn when he mocked controversial U.S. secretary of Health
body:
John Mulaney‘s opening monologue on this week’s “Saturday Night Live” took an unexpected turn when he mocked controversial U.S. secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

	The comic started by impersonating Kennedy, saying, “‘My father was a good man and I’m a lousy man but I have same name. Am I good if I have same name as father? No, please, let me be in charge of your bones and your tummy. Please allow me to control how your blood feels in your butt and everywhere. Stop the science … Robitussin when taken during menstruation will cause telekinesis. This is clear from the pamphlets in my rental car.’”
	

	Mulaney then slammed Kennedy’s vaccine skepticism, saying, “No one likes him. You dumbass … your thing can’t be the measles!”

	He then mocked Kennedy’s previous occupation as an environmental lawyer, saying, “He would just join cases late if they were about be successful. ‘Are you about to win? I’m part of this too.’” 

	Mulaney then described the times he interacted with the politician by doing comedy at benefits for Kennedy’s Riverkeepers organization.

	“They were in charge of keeping the Hudson River in New York City clean,” Mulaney said. “That was his job. That’s how good he is at jobs. His old job was keeping the Hudson River, whose native fish is tied-off used condom, clean. Now he’s in charge of all of our tummies.”

	The Nov. 14 episode was Mulaney’s seventh as host. His monologue also touched on family issues and children whose deep, scratchy voices remind him of Kennedy.
	

	Watch Mulaney’s full monologue below.

schema.headline: John Mulaney Mocks Robert F. Kennedy Jr. in ‘SNL’ Monologue: ‘No One Likes Him. You Dumbass … Your Thing Can’t Be the Measles!’

title: Amanda Seyfried to Make Her Debut as ‘Saturday Night Live’ Host
description:
Amanda Seyfried will make her debut as host of “Saturday Night Live” on Dec. 5.

	Seyfried is center stage in one of the year’s most talked-about m
body:
Amanda Seyfried will make her debut as host of “Saturday Night Live” on Dec. 5.

	Seyfried is center stage in one of the year’s most talked-about movies, the Elizabeth Holmes documentary “You Can See Everything.” The musical guest for the episode will be rapper Don Toliver.

	“SNL” confirmed Seyfried’s gig with a graphic flashed during the Nov. 14 episode, hosted by John Mulaney.


	Seyfried has a big role in A24’s “You Can See Everything” given her history of playing the convicted Theranos fraudster Holmes in the 2022 Hulu limited series “The Dropout.” Directors Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim tapped Seyfried to recreate some scenes in a meta approach to the doc that chronicles the final few weeks for Holmes before she begins her prison sentence for her conviction on multiple charges of wire fraud.
	

	Seyfried recently completed the indie film “The Life and Deaths of Winston Shedd,” opposite Tim Blake Nelson. She’s also set to voice the lead role of Cinderella in Netflix’s upcoming animated film “Steps.” She had a busy year in 2025 with starring roles in two successful films, Paul Feig’s “The Housemaid” and Mona Fastvold’s “The Testament of Ann Lee.”

	Seyfried earned an Oscar nomination for supporting actress for her work in David Fincher’s 2021 drama “Mank,” about screenwriter Herman Mankiewicz and the making of Orson Welles’ 1941 movie masterpiece “Citizen Kane.” She was nominated for an Emmy for her work in “The Dropout.” 

	Toliver is a singer and rapper out of the Houston area who has seen his star rise over the past half-dozen years. At present he’s in the midst of touring the U.K.

schema.headline: Amanda Seyfried to Make Her Debut as ‘Saturday Night Live’ Host

title: Bowen Yang Returns to ‘SNL’ as Jensen Huang as John Mulaney’s Cold Open Mocks Nvidia Scandal, National Ground Stop and Outlook Outage
description: Bowen Yang made a surprise return to “Saturday Night Live” in the cold open, playing the disgraced tech mogul Jensen Huang as host John Mulaney led
body:
Bowen Yang made a surprise return to “Saturday Night Live” in the cold open, playing the disgraced tech mogul Jensen Huang as host John Mulaney led a group of tech billionaires through a CIA class on how to recognize female spies. 

	The cold open featured Mulaney as a CIA agent who gathered ultra-rich tech moguls at the agency’s headquarters for a crash course on how to recognize a classic espionage honeytrap, a nod to the Nvidia scandal that has rocked the business world. In the closing moments of the sketch, former “SNL” trouper Yang walked in delivering a pitch-perfect spoof of Huang, who was forced under pressure to resign on Nov. 12 from the Silicon Valley giant that he built for more than 30 years amid a growing sex scandal.
	

	Yang introduced himself “Jensen Hide-Your-Wife Huang.” Yang as Huang lamented that “women don’t like guys like us. That’s how we became guys like us,” after Mulaney’s CIA agent flashes him Venn diagram charts that show no overlap between beautiful women and tech billionaires. Yang also quipped that when Huang comes into the room, “You know what’s about to go down — the S&P 500.” And in a nod to Nvidia’s heft in the stock market, he added: “That’s right — I’m in to BDSM: Breaking the stock market.”

	The sketch featured “SNL regulars playing the tech billionaires who have flexed so much power over politics and culture in recent years. James Austin Johnson played Peter Thiel, Andrew Dismukes limned Mark Zuckerberg, Jane Wickline played Anthropic chief Dario Amodei, Jeremy Culhane inhabited Elon Musk and Ben Marshall spoofed OpenAI chief Sam Altman.
	

	In a CIA conference room setting, Mulaney’s CIA agent used a pointer and monitor to flash Venn diagram graphics to school the billionaires in the difference between “Woman who would actualy want to have sex with you” and “A woman who is clearly a spy.” The sketch turned on the story that has made global headlines as Huang admitted to have a romantic relationship with a woman who is believed to be a spy for China. In the days since the scandal broke, allegations surfaced that Huang, who is married, had relationships with two employees at Nvidia.

	“Never date a human woman,” Dismukes as Zuckerberg said of the lesson to draw from the Nvidia scandal. “Never date anyone lest they become the antichrist,” Johnson as Thiel offered. 


	Thiel defended the contributions of tech billionaires to the greater good and asked Mulaney to “name one time when technology has let us down?” Mulaney cited this week’s one-two punch of the massive disruptions that exposed the vulnerabilities of our wired world: The five-hour national ground stop on air travel on Friday and Microsoft’s widely used email platform Outlook experiencing a global outage for nearly 24 hours. 

	“Like yesterday when every plane was grounded? Or the day before when Microsoft Outlook went dark?” Mulaney said.

	Altman questioned whether he and Thiel, who are gay, needed the training to detect female spies. Johnson as Thiel added “and we are both bears in the sense that we’ve killed a lot of hikers.”

	Mulaney is notching his seventh time as host of “SNL,” after working on the show as a writer from 2008 to He’s in the midst of a push for Amazon Prime Video’s John Madden biopic “Madden,” which bows on the streamer and in limited theatrical release on Nov. 18. He’s also touring at present on his “Mister Whatever” stand-up tour. Mulaney most recently took the helm in November 2024.

	Phoebe Bridgers will perform as “SNL” musical guest for the second time. She’s currently on tour with her newest album “Lost Weekend.”

schema.headline: Bowen Yang Returns to ‘SNL’ as Jensen Huang as John Mulaney’s Cold Open Mocks Nvidia Scandal, National Ground Stop and Outlook Outage

title: Brandi Carlile’s All-Requests Tour Isn’t Just a Magnificent Stunt, but an Unusually Moving Transaction Between Performer and Audience: Concert Review
description: Is it possible to plan for magic, serendipity, peak-level proficiency and finally sublimity by… really not planning at all? That is the question.
body:
Is it possible to plan for magic, serendipity, peak-level proficiency and finally sublimity by… really not planning at all? That is the question. On Brandi Carlile‘s current “Burn the Setlist!” tour, the answer is clear: Sometimes Shangri-La really is best reached with a lost roadmap.

	The shortish 19-date outing Carlile is undertaking at the moment is the first all-requests tour in memory by any artist significant enough to have it show up on our radar. It might even be a historic first, as far as a proven headliner opting to play nothing but spontaneously generated live audience picks. Which is odd when you think about it, because doesn’t anyone who’s been to a lot of shows over the years have a favorite moment when a star got loose and succumbed to someone shouting out a favorite (though they usually don’t want to encourage that kind of behavior?). But at the opposite end of the scale from bar bands and tip jars, doing solely requests sounds like as much of a nightmare to most performers as it does a dream to hardcore fans. There are perfectly good reasons not to throw the song selections completely open to stans for roughly 2 hours and 40 minutes — as Carlile and her two bandmates, Phil and Tim Hanseroth, are doing now — when you have a recorded catalog of close to a hundred original songs, plus a repertoire of proven live cover choices.

	Who among even the greats of music has anything close to 100% recall? When the recent and distant pasts are both being dredged up, a good corollary to “Never let ’em see you sweat” might be: Never let ’em see you forget.

	Fortunately, Brandi Carlile and the Hanseroth twins are freaking elephants.



	

					Brandi Carlile in Oakland at the Fox Theatre
									Jen Horton
	



	But making a point out of not planning is different from not being prepared. And Carlile and the brothers are prepared for this, first of all, by having brain chemistry that is clearly a little bit different from mine or probably yours, with the power not just to generate constant creative sparks but to put those sparks in an easily accessible lockbox. You’re either genetically predisposed to that kind of recall or you’re not, and at least a little part of why Carlile and the Hanseroths have been ideal partners since the turn of the millennium is that shared gift. Not that they came into the “Burn the Setlist!” tour relying completely on muscle memory. Tim Hanseroth posted an IG video of himself running through their studio albums and strumming along to stir the old juices. Carlile said in a video livestream for fans on the tour’s eve that she would have a monitor for lyrics if she needed it. But at the show I caught, I barely noticed Carlile looking down at it… which I can’t say for most big tours I attend where the show is locked in for months straight.

	All of this risks making the tour seem like a stunt, which it kind of is. But the bigger reason for why it’s such a rousing success — and a reason why fans may remember these shows almost as well as Carlile and company remember their songs — is how many deeply moving moments are stirred up up in the shows, in the quietest bits that come between the outbreaks of hysterical shouting and sign-waving. Leaving the setlists up to fans, chance or God results in obscure picks and ironic juxtapositions that sometimes aren’t anything more than fun or curious, but are sometimes unexpectedly touching in a way that one of Carlile’s perfectly laid-out arena shows probably couldn’t be. Not just a mere test of skills, these concerts are really a nightly emotional chemistry experiment. On the right night — and the show I saw in Oakland was the right night — it might be transcendent, in a way that’s a little different even from the transcendent gigs we’ve seen before.


	Carlile had some notes before the show began; rather than restrictions, felt like promissory instructions about how to best proceed through a candy store about to open. “I can see your signs all the way back, and I will call on people all the way in the back,” Carlile declared at the top of the concert Nov. 7 at the Fox Oakland, the second on their tour. (She later made good on that, picking more people from the rear balcony than any other part of the audience, though the front rows did OK too.).”Everything is pretty much fair game,” she instructed — “any song that we’ve ever done.” She noted that they wouldn’t be open to attempting songs they’d never performed even once before, “so we’re not gonna be able to ‘Free Bird’ or ‘Sweet Home Alabama’ this shit. But we might be able to get away with the handful of covers we’ve done in the past. And listen,” she added reassuringly, “you don’t have to worry about me — I’m 45, so if there’s a song I don’t want to do, I will just say no.”

	But Carlile also wanted it understood that this was not meant to be a tricky pop quiz. “Don’t feel like this should be a ‘stump the band’-type deal,” she said. “We really want this to be musically awesome for you guys. We want you to love what you’re hearing and request the songs that you really want to hear. I’m a deep cuts girl. I love track 7 on everyone’s album. I’m a last track gal. And I know that you know that you’re never gonna hear those songs on the big tours that we do.” That said, she opened it up to the idea that predictability isn’t always a negative. “If you want to hear the fucking ‘Story,'” Carlile declared, “just request ‘The Story’!”


	No one chosen in Oakland wanted to choose the fucking “Story,” or “The Joke” or anything else that might qualify as too big a hit, possibly in fear of eliciting groans from a rarities-inclined audience. (It does feel safe to call her biggest songs hits, even if toward the end, listening to the roars for obscurities, she said, “It almost makes up for the fact that we never had a hit. If you’ve never had a hit, all your songs get to be hits with your buddies. I don’t think we need one.”) But Carlile stating her openness to doing more predictable songs did create a safety net for the audience, establishing that there would be no wrong answers or incorrect pleas.
	

	Also no duds, although one song choice did pose an unsolved mystery, with its unexpected popularity, which was resolved with a bit of discussion between performers and audience. A couple in the front row of the Fox Oakland’s balcony requested “Heart’s Content,” which got only light applayse Carlile then noted had also been requested the previous night in Portland… to her puzzlement. “I think this song’s gonna be requested every night,” she laughed, “because we never play it and it’s to me the most obscure song. Is it even on one of our albums?” It is — from 14 years ago — but it’s understandable why it’s never been a concert favorite: Perfectly pleasant-sounding, it’s the rare tune in her 21-year catalog that just doesn’t really sound like a Brandi Carlile. Phil Hanseroth relayed reportage from someone in the front rows: “It’s in a movie.” “What’s the movie?” “Safe Haven.” “Is it a romcom?” inquired Carlile. “Is it sad, like ‘The Notebook?’ Well, thank you — now I understand… A bunch of romcom fans up in here.” No judgments.
	

	There was a greater sense of consensus, on-stage and off-, about most of the rest of the 22 songs played in Oakland. The first chosen was “Raising Hell,” a rowdy oldie that made it clear that, among other things, Carlile and the twins have always harbored stomp-and-holler tendencies… with literal stomping, on a few occasions in this set, to add percussion into the mix. In the most extreme pendulum swing possible, next up among the requests was a song about raising heaven, “The Mother,” a gorgeously happy song that deals with motherhood very generally and gay motherhood very specifically.

	Carlile preceded “The Mother” with an extended anecdote about chaperoning the social life of her eldest daughter, who’s repeatedly named in the chorus — with a side note that the story should not leave the room, since Evangeline is at the age where it’s not easy to always discern whether she resents being talked about on stage or takes pride in it in any given moment. That alone, in the singer’s mind, justified the decision to have phones put away in Yondr pouches, something Carlile has not required at any of her previous gigs but wanted for these, both to create greater intimacy and to keep flubs from going up on YouTube. (There weren’t any blatant ones, although the Hanseroths did shoot knowing smiles at each other a couple of times when a note sounded a little bit interesting.)

	Carlile has often spoken before “The Mother” in concert, but the loose formatting of this show seemed to allow her to stretch out even more, over a period of minutes. “I remember having a really difficult time with it because Catherine carried both girls… Somebody talked me through it and told me I needed to come up with a mantra. And my mantra became, I have to tell myself I’m a mother so that I can believe I deserve to call myself that. So it became ‘I am the mother of Evangeline.’ And when I first wrote this song, I thought, ‘Well, this thing’s niche! You have to be a gay mom that didn’t carry a child to understand this song.’ And it’s not true — it’s a universal thing — because here I am in Oakland, and this man stood up and wanted me to play the song.”

	The mood swings got wilder from there, as “Folsom Prison Blues” was requested next, a cover Carlile figured they hadn’t done in a decade. (Actually, only seven years.) The twins spent a bit of time remember and working out the licks before a formal kickoff that led to some wildly exuberant death in Reno. From there, in another big turnabout, it was “Dying Day,” which they opted to do at the lip of the stage, without amplification, as they’d done in the distant past, albeit probably in slightly smaller rooms than the 2,800-capacity Fox. Voices carried.
	

	The tour offers an opportunity to witness problem-solving in real time. For Carlile and the twins, perhaps the biggest problem was obliging a request for Alanis Morissette’s “Uninvited.” This was not because of recent unfamiliarity with the tune — they performed it nearly every night on this year’s “Human” arena tour, among the encores — but because they’d never done it as an acoustic trio. Without the heightened drama of a string section and the number’s signature piano notes. “I have no idea how we’re gonna do this without strings. Love will find a way,” Carlile said. “And no piano? That’s the whole song!” But she and the brothers found their path to make it a pure guitar-and-bass rock ‘n’ roll scorcher, followed by an exultant “We don’t need no stinking strings!” (With implicit apologies, undoubtedly, to SistaStrings.)



	

					Brandi Carlile in Oakland at the Fox Theatre
	



	“I Belong With You” was introduced as having been written “when I first met my wife, Catherine… I wasn’t a big love song girl. I didn’t really get them.” The monologue was interrupted when she went to greet a young girl in the front row who was having her own emotional moment. Hi babe. What’s goin’ on?… Don’t cry!” When she came back, she dropped the love-story intro, but did have some instructions for the Hanseroths: “You guys aren’t on in this one until four minutes.” They took five for four, and you didn’t have to look at your watch — but just for fun, I did — to know that she was right on target with her reminder to the bros, give or take 10 seconds. This was a woman who knows her own material, as was repeatedly evident when each request was immediately followed by a callout to her guitar tech about which instrument to bring out. (“That’s gonna be capo 8 for a strummer”… “‘That Year’ is gonna be Kalamazoo, capo 7.”)

	Carlile sang “Turpentine,” a song about physically battling with her brother growing up, with its wistful rejoinder, “I’m warning you, we’re growing up” — and though she didn’t directly make the connection this night, it was easy to surmise how growing up to close to her “Irish twin” brother prepared her for a life and career with the Hanseroth twins. She taled about writing “Stranger at My Door” in Australia, “jetlagged with a broken heart,” and bringing the new song to the twins in a club’s backstage alley. “‘Tell me the truth. Is it too much? Is it too many words?’ Phil’s like, ‘Eh, it’s a little wordy.’ Phil’s a 7 on the Enneogram. You know what that means?… You’re incredibly impatient, and this song is five minutes long and full of words and that’s why you guys love it!” she laughed, turning to the attending Bramily.
	

	Dolly Parton was saluted with “Jolene” — “She had a temper, she had a dirty mouth, and she had the biggest heart in the world,” said Carlile — and a call-out for some Joni Mitchell on that singer’s birthday went rewarded with an E-major “River.” The singer talked about a two-and-a-half-hour phone call while driving home on Halloween night, hearing even more wild stories from the legend than she’d already heard. “A lot of times she’ll end the story by going, ‘And that was where I found “Refuge of the Roads.”‘ Or, ‘And that’s why I shouldn’t have got on that plane.’ In those moments, I realized that, no matter what happens in my life, I got to listen to Joni Mitchell play solitaire and tell me her stories. She’s not lying. I’m not even sure she’s capable of it.”

	The last stretch of the Oakland concert lifted the show from delightful travelogue to a something heavier on some of the trio’s most emotionally incisive songs, although it was difficult to know whether they were making these selections intentionally or those requests were providentially just arriving right on time. Tim Hanseroth did say he’d been waiting all night to pick on the guy in the front rows holding a sign asking for “The Things I Regret,” and subsequently showed up on Instagram thanking the fan again. It raised one of those questions that can only arise at a rarities-filled show like this: Why was this not a bigger hit — even amongst the band itself? It’s got an unforgettable singalong hook and serious stomp-and-holler bona fides, and it’s about the accumulation of screw-ups that adds up to a lifetime’s worth. What more could you ask?



	

					Brandi Carlile in Oakland at the Fox Theatre
									Jen Horton
	



	But the most touching highlights were “Most of All,” a song about seeing your family in yourself (there are few lines more evocative than “His heavy hands swing at the end of my arms”)… and “That Year,” an alternately chilling and warm ballad about looking to make peace with a high school friend who committed suicide, from across the veil that separates the living and the dead. And the recent “No One Knows Us,” about how each friendship bond formed among young people is precious, irreplaceable and worth the upkeep in a more depressed middle age. And the penultimate number, “That Wasn’t Me,” a neo-gospel ballad so healing and cathartic, it would have become Carlile’s signature song in some other lifetime, instead of a deep cut.

	The actual climax? A rare cover of Led Zeppelin’s “Going to California,” because Carlile can hit the golden-god notes. And then California surrendered the combo to the next stop in Tucson. (Where they did not get the Led out, of course, and where the next stop involved only repeating four of the 22 numbers heard in Oakland.)
	

	As a cherry on top, anyone leaving the show each night finds that there was a bonus offered earlier, not to them, but to anyone suffering at home with FOMO. Right before she takes the stage, when the local audience is already seated, Carlile does a livestream of a single song while she’s having her makeup applied, just for everyone who doesn’t have the privilege of the live show (though, of course, the concert crowd can catch up with it later). It’s a hell of a miniature grace note.

	Saying this was the best show I’ve ever seen by Carlile and company probably without saying, after saying all of that; at times, I got to thinking it was one of the best shows I’ve ever seen from anyone, out of untold thousands. Concert hyperbole is a dangerous thing, but I found myself hard-pressed to recall comparable instances in which I’d seen rock ‘n’ roll performers so throughly committed to the moment, not just for a moment but for close to three hours of them. Maybe that’s because I have a worse memory than Carlile and the Hanseroths, but more likely because this really is as good as it gets, if you have a taste for the rare intersection where hair-trigger meets tear-jerk. Adjust your settings for how many hundreds of dollars you’d pay for a resale ticket for the remaining dates accordingly.



	

					Brandi Carlile in Oakland at the Fox Theatre
									Jen Horton
	



	Setlist for Brandi Carlile at the Fox Oakland, November 2026:
	

	Raise HellThe MotherFolsom Prison Blues (Johnny Cash cover)Dying DayHeart’s ContentUninvited (Alanis Morissette cover)I Belong to YouHumanTurpentineHard Way HomeI WillThe Stranger at My DoorMost of AllJolene (Dolly Parton cover)That YearRiver (Joni Mitchell cover)The Things I RegretCloser to You/I’ve Just Seen a Face (Beatles cover)No One Knows UsBeginning to Feel the YearsThat Wasn’t MeGoing to California (Led Zeppelin)

title: High School Football Player Dies After Being Declared Brain Dead Following Collapse

body:

                          Dies After Being Declared Brain Dead, Gym Collapse
                      
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            A high school student who collapsed in the middle of gym class has died after the medical emergency left him brain dead.
      
    
            Levi Curry -- who was a rising defensive star on the Eagle River High School football team in Anchorage, Alaska -- went into cardiac arrest during the gym class on Nov. 6 ... according to his GoFundMe.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Later that night, Levi was declared brain dead.
      

            Apparently, Levi suffered from a pre-existing heart condition that was managed by a pediatric cardiologist ... his church shared.
      
    
            Levi's dad James told KTUU that his son had undergone surgery that "basically healed it."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            After his parents made the tough decision to proceed with organ donation, Levi died on Nov. 7.
      
    
            Nearly 500 people showed up to pay their respects at Levi's funeral ... PEOPLE reported.
      
    
            He was only 15 years old.

title: Over 720K BMW Vehicles Recalled Over Fire Risk
description:
Major BMW Recall
                          Over 720,000 Vehicles Affected
body:
Major BMW Recall
                          Over 720,000 Vehicles Affected
                          Turn Them Off, Now!
                      
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            A whopping 720,796 BMWs have been recalled over the risk of a fire ... as officials urge owners to turn their cars off and leave them parked.
      
    
            Apparently, the issue lies with an improperly sealed electrical connector located on the water pump ... according to a safety alert by the NHTSA.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            If the connector gets exposed to water, it could short-circuit and cause a fire.
      

            The NHTSA stressed ... "If you have one of these vehicles, you should park your vehicle outside and away from buildings and other vehicles until the vehicle is repaired."
      
    
            So far, they've only experienced 10 incidents related to the issue ... but better safe than sorry!
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The models affected include:
      
    
            2012-2016 3 Series, 2012-2016 5 Series, 2012–2015 X1, 2012-2016 Z4, 2013-2017 X3, 2014-2016 2 Series coupe, 2014–2016 3 Series sportswagon, 2014-2016 328xi Gran Turismo, 2014-2016 4 Series convertible, 2014-2016 4 Series coupe, 2015-2016 2 Series convertible, 2015-2016 4 Series gran coupe, 2015-2018 X4, and 2016-2018 X5 xDrive40e.
      
    
            This isn't the first time these vehicles have been recalled either ... apparently they had another water pump issue back in 2024.
